methodological_questions: How to measure lineup coverage from player role categories
How to isolate within-team coverage variation from roster composition and player counts
How to control for overall talent without circularity
What confounding factors affect the estimated effect of coverage on offensive efficiency
How to verify that talent control behaves as expected
evidence_establishes: Role categories (Primary Organizer, Shaper, Terminal Scorer) can be assigned per player per team-season using initiation and structural influence as defined in prior project work
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies meaningfully within a team
Whether any such variation is separable from simply counting high-usage players or from aggregate talent metrics
That talent control variables behave stably and predictably when testing a coverage hypothesis
Any previous design or pilot results specific to lineup coverage
own_inferences: The required data (per-game play-by-play, substitution intervals, player-level initiation records) is sufficient to compute structural fingerprints and role categories for each team-season
Lineup coverage can be defined as a binary stent-level variable: a stint has coverage if the five players on court together include at least one Primary Organizer, one Shaper, and one Terminal Scorer

Within-team variation is possible only if the team roster contains at least one player of each category and the rotation sometimes places them on the bench together; if all lineups always have coverage there is no variation to test

Separability from talent/counts can be tested by adding aggregated player talent (offensive EPM or RAPM) and simple counts of each role category on the floor to a regression of stint-level points per possession on coverage
'Talent control behaves' likely means that the talent coefficient is positive, stable across model specifications, and does not change sign erratically when coverage is included
uncertainties: The distribution of role categories across rosters and lineups; some teams may have no Shaper, making coverage impossible by definition, or may always field all three roles
Stability of role assignments across a season; roles are derived from full-season usage and influence which could introduce endogeneity if the same games are used for the coverage test
The appropriate talent metric and whether a single-number summary (e.g., sum of offensive EPM) adequately captures the skill components most relevant to coverage
The minimal stint length needed for reliable PPP estimation and the resulting effective sample size
Whether the mechanical requirement of needing at least three distinct role players creates a floor effect that confounds interpretation of coverage coefficients

historical_effect.explanation: No prior study on this specific question was returned, so the decision is based entirely on data availability, conceptual reasoning, and risk assessment.

blocking_constraints.text: Within-team variation in coverage may be rare if most lineups naturally contain at least one organizer, shaper, and terminal. If the proportion of stints lacking coverage is very low, statistical power to detect an effect will be insufficient.

Player role categories depend on usage and residual structural influence thresholds. For players near the median or with few initiations, classification can be noisy, leading to misclassification of coverage status.

The coverage definition requires at least three specific role players on the floor. If a team roster lacks any of those roles entirely, all stints are uncovered by construction, eliminating variation. Even when roles exist, natural substitution patterns may enforce a coverage floor.

Role categories are correlated with player skill; shapers and organizers tend to be better players. Controlling for talent with a single metric may leave residual confounding, making it difficult to isolate pure 'coverage' from general player quality.

prior_work.summary: No earlier project study on lineup coverage was retrieved. The role framework exists and is operational, but the specific hypothesis has not been tested.

risks.text: Limited within-team variation in coverage may render estimates imprecise or inestimable.
Role misclassification attenuates the coverage signal and can bias coefficients.
If roles are defined using the same games in which coverage is tested, extreme role realizations may regress, creating spurious associations.
Role categories are derived from initiation patterns that are part of the offensive efficiency measure; using them as regressors risks circularity unless roles are estimated from prior data.
Omitted variable bias from unmeasured aspects of player skill or coach strategy may confound the coverage effect.
Teams with very imbalanced rosters may never achieve coverage, and those that always have it offer no variation; the floor effect complicates inference.
Testing coverage across many team-seasons inflates the chance of false positives unless adjusted.
Role categories may shift over the season due to player development, injuries, or coaching changes, violating the assumption of static roles.

design.estimand: The causal effect of stent-level lineup coverage (binary: >=1 Primary Organizer, >=1 Shaper, >=1 Terminal Scorer) on offense-only points per possession (PPP), controlling for aggregated player talent and the counts of each role type present.
design.unit: Stint (continuous interval of fixed ten players), filtered to a minimum of 3 possessions and excluding garbage time.
design.sample: All regular-season stints from NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26. Separate secondary analyses for playoffs and for first-vs-second half to check consistency.
design.power: Simulation-based power analysis using 2022-23 to 2024-25 data: estimate the intra-team standard deviation of coverage status, compute the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) for a within-team partial correlation at 80% power, and proceed only if MDES is plausible (e.g., < 0.02 PPP). If within-team variation is too scarce, pool teams in a hierarchical model and report MDES for the overall average effect.
design.controls: Game- and quarter-fixed effects, point differential at stint start (binned), sum of offensive EPM or multi-year RAPM for the five offensive players, and count of each role category present (organizers, shapers, terminals). A robustness check adds interactions between talent and role counts.
design.falsification: 1) Role-permutation placebo: randomly reassign roles within each team-season 10,000 times and check that the true coverage coefficient lies outside the 95th percentile of the null distribution. 2) Test the coverage effect on defensive PPP, where no mechanism predicts a positive effect; any finding there would suggest residual talent confound. 3) Garbage-time validation: coverage effect should attenuate in garbage time if it reflects strategic coherence.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register a single primary hypothesis test on the average coverage coefficient from a hierarchical Bayesian model with team-level random slopes. Report team-specific effects with 95% credible intervals after applying a Benjamini-Hochberg correction across teams as an exploratory output.
design.decision_rule: Coverage is judged separable from talent if its posterior probability of being positive exceeds 0.975 after controlling for talent and role counts, and if the talent coefficient remains positive and stable (no sign reversal across 95% of posterior draws) across all pre-registered model specifications. 'Talent control behaves' is verified if the talent coefficient's sign aligns with prior knowledge and its inclusion does not flip the coverage coefficient's sign.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files as of 2026-07-13, play-by-play and substitution data, with player-level structural fingerprints and roles derived from the project graph database using the 2022-23 through 2025-26 seasons.

methodological_questions: separating coverage from counts and talent
args.query: lineup coverage defined as >=1 organizer, shaper, terminal varies within team separable from talent counts

TOOL_RESULT glossary:
# Terminology used in the research questions

This glossary is given identically in every condition. It defines terms only and reports no results. Definitions follow the published papers (Structural Influence; Detecting Defensive Suppression) where they exist.

- **Possession, PPP:** a team's continuous spell with the ball; PPP is points per possession.
- **H1, H2:** first half (periods 1 and 2) and second half (periods 3 and 4) of a game. RS and PO: regular season and playoffs.
- **Play type:** the label assigned to each possession by the project's rule-based classifier from play-by-play events. Labels include PNR (pick-and-roll ball handler), DRIVE, CUT, SPOT_UP, PULL_UP, POST_UP, PUTBACK and TRANSITION. A play-type mix is a team's share of possessions in each play type.
- **Initiator, initiation:** the offensive player whose action starts the possession's play type (for example the cutter on a cut, the ball handler on a pick-and-roll). Initiation records are possession-level rows linking initiator, play type and points.
- **Inferrer:** the classifier step that infers a play type (for example a pick-and-roll) from play-by-play text when it is not recorded directly.
- **Suppression trigger:** a team, play type and game in which the team's PPP on that play type falls sharply from H1 to H2 under fixed minimum-attempt rules; read as the defense possibly taking the action away.
- **Continuation, counter:** after a trigger, continuation means the offense keeps running the triggered play type; a counter is a different play type run instead.
- **BEST, AVOID (counter tiers):** the strategy app's matchup-ranked counter recommendations after a trigger. BEST is the top-ranked counter play type for that matchup, AVOID the lowest-ranked.
- **Structural fingerprint:** a team's standardized pattern of how play types share initiators.
- **Structural influence (load, L):** how much a team's structural fingerprint changes when one player's initiations are removed. L_pre is that quantity measured from games before an absence.
- **Usage:** a player's share of team possessions he initiates or finishes.
- **Role categories (Structural Influence paper):** by crossing usage (above or below the rotation median) with residual influence (structural influence beyond what usage predicts): Primary Organizer (high usage, positive residual), Shaper (low usage, positive residual), Terminal Scorer (high usage, residual at or below zero), Role Occupant or Specialist (low usage, residual at or below zero).
- **Connector:** a structural-role label used in later studies for players whose presence links teammates' play types; the exact rule varied between studies.
- **Hub:** a high-structural-influence player around whom a team's initiations are organized.
- **Absence spell:** a run of consecutive games a player misses (the main studies used at least 15).
- **Displacement (D_real):** how far teammates' play-type mix moves during an absence spell relative to before it (one minus the cosine similarity of the two mixes).
- **Mover, decoy:** a mover is a player who changed teams between seasons; decoys are comparison players used as placebo matches for a mover.
- **Stint:** an interval of play with the same ten players on the court.
- **Garbage time:** late-game possessions with a lopsided score, usually excluded.

We need to fill in the stage-2 output. First, we have the retrieval result: empty list. So no historical evidence or failed approaches from retrieve_history. We need to proceed with steps 4-9.

Let's parse the research question: "Lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves."

The question seems to be about "lineup coverage" defined as having at least one organizer, one shaper, and one terminal scorer on the floor. So a lineup's coverage is a binary condition: does the lineup have at least one player of each of these three role categories? The question: "Lineup coverage ... varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves." I interpret it as: we want to test whether lineup coverage (i.e., having all three roles represented) varies meaningfully within a team (i.e., not all lineups are the same), and whether this variation can be separated from simply counting the number of players on the floor (obviously 5 players, but coverage requires at least 3 specific role types; perhaps "counts" means total number of players of a given role category available? Or maybe "counts" means the sheer number of high-usage players? Unclear). Also, "talent control behaves" likely means that if we control for overall talent (player quality metrics), the effect of coverage remains distinct.

The methodological questions: How to measure lineup coverage? How to isolate its variation within team? How to control for talent? What confounders exist? Is coverage variation independent of talent/counts? etc.

Historical evidence: none returned.

Now we need to produce the output. We have to assess testability, risks, decision.

First, what data is available? NBA per-game files: play-by-play, substitution intervals, starters, defensive matchups, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points). So we have player-level initiation data, which can be used to compute structural influence and assign role categories (Primary Organizer, Shaper, Terminal Scorer, Role Occupant) using the rules from the papers. That seems possible. Then for each lineup (a stint with specific players on court), we can check if at least one player of each role category is present. The categories are defined per player based on usage and residual influence relative to team rotation median, presumably computed over the whole season or a window. The research question: "varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves." That suggests a hypothesis that within a team, different lineups have different coverage (some have all three roles, some don't), and that this variation is not simply driven by the presence of a few high-talent players (i.e., you could have high-talent players who are all of one type, and coverage still matters). And talent control behaves: perhaps that means adjusting for a summary talent metric (like aggregate EPM or RAPM) still leaves coverage predictive of offensive efficiency.

Testability: The data can produce player-level role classifications for each team-season. Then for each possession or stint, we can map players to their pre-assigned roles and determine coverage. However, a key issue: roles are derived from volume of initiation and structural influence; these are outcomes themselves. So if we then use coverage to predict points per possession or other outcomes, there might be circularity: roles are defined by initiation patterns, which may be influenced by who is on the court. That is a potential confounder: MEASURE_RELIABILITY, maybe LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD if roles are computed from the same games we are testing. Could be RTM_SELECTION if we define roles based on performance, causing regression to the mean. The question says "is separable from talent/counts" – that implies we need to control for talent. But we can compute player talent from external metrics (e.g., EPM) to avoid circularity. That might be doable.

Also, "talent control behaves" – what does that mean? Possibly that controlling for talent yields a plausible coefficient (not erratic), i.e., it behaves as expected. That is more of a diagnostic than a testable hypothesis.

Risks: 
- SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER: Within-team variation may be limited if teams rarely deviate from having all three roles on the floor. The coverage condition is at least one organizer, one shaper, one terminal. In a typical lineup, you'd probably have at least one high-usage player (organizer or terminal) and some shapers. But some teams might always have all three roles covered, so within-team variation could be sparse. That's EXPOSURE_SPARSITY.
- MEASURE_RELIABILITY: Role assignment depends on usage threshold and residual influence; these are estimated with noise, especially for players with few possessions. Could result in misclassification.
- CONFOUNDING: Talent and role categories are correlated; high-usage players may be better scorers. If we control for talent with a single metric, residual confounding may persist.
- OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL: Role categories derived from the same outcomes we might want to predict.
- LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD: If roles are computed from full season, and we test within-season, it's fine, but if we want to test predictive power, need to avoid lookahead. The question doesn't explicitly state prediction, but "separable from talent/counts" suggests a causal or descriptive analysis, not prediction.
- MECHANICAL_FLOOR: The coverage criterion (>=1 of each) imposes a floor: you need at least 3 players to get coverage. By definition, a lineup of 5 players will have coverage if the team has at least one player of each role available. If a team has no player of a certain role category (e.g., no shaper), then no lineup can have coverage. So within-team variation is only possible if the team has at least one of each role category and sometimes they are not all on the floor at the same time. This could be driven by roster composition, not lineup strategy.
- RTM_SELECTION: If roles are defined based on outlier performance, those players may regress, causing apparent coverage effects to be artifacts.
- MULTIPLE_TESTING: If testing many teams, need adjustment.

Now, testability: I'd say it's likely testable with careful design, but with substantial risks. p_testable maybe 0.6.

Design: We need to propose a plan. estimand: The effect of having lineup coverage (binary) on offensive points per possession, controlling for talent and number of each role category (counts). Unit: stint-level or possession-level? Could be stint-level: each stint is a continuous interval with same players, can compute PPP for that stint, and coverage status. But stint length varies; many stints short. Power analysis would be needed. sample: 2022-23 to 2025-26 NBA data. Exclude garbage time, maybe playoffs separate. controls: team fixed effects, season, quarter, game score margin (to account for game situation), and talent metrics: sum of player-level EPM or RAPM (offensive), and counts of organizers, shapers, terminals on floor (above coverage threshold). Also control for whether the three required roles are available at all (roster availability indicator). falsification: use placebo roles (random assignment) or test on a previous season where we shouldn't see effects? Or test if the coverage effect disappears when controlling for an interaction. Design decision rule: if coverage coefficient is positive and significant (p<0.05 after multiple comparison correction) and the effect persists after adding talent controls, then coverage matters. But we also need to check that the coefficient on talent controls behaves as expected (positive, stable). That addresses "talent control behaves". Multiplicity: will test across many team-seasons; use hierarchical model or FDR.

Predicted outcome: given historical evidence is absent, but my own reasoning: likelihood of finding a robust effect is uncertain; might be artifact due to role definitions. I'd assign 0.2 supported, 0.2 rejected, 0.4 untestable (data might be insufficient due to lack of variation), 0.1 artifact, 0.1 uncertain. Actually, "untestable" would be if we cannot measure coverage variation reliably; "artifact" if an effect appears but is due to bias. I'll adjust.

Now, the stage-2 output must include historical_evidence and failed_approaches as empty lists. evidence_establishes and evidence_does_not_establish: we can say that no prior study directly examined this specific hypothesis. The project's previous work on structural roles established role categories and structural influence, but not coverage. So evidence establishes that role categorization is feasible; evidence does not establish whether lineup coverage varies within team or is separable from talent. own_inferences: we can infer that the necessary data is available; the main challenge is defining roles non-circularly and ensuring sufficient variation. uncertainties: about distribution of role categories across lineups, about stability of roles over season, about the appropriate talent metric, about potential for mechanical floor (roster composition).
